title: The Dare Ladder
tagline: One harmless dare. Keep adding rungs until the ladder wobbles.
premise: You and a friend are building one ridiculous dare, rung by rung. Start with a harmless dare, then take turns adding exactly one harder rule while keeping every earlier rule. If your rung breaks the ladder, you lose suddenly. Keep it safe, doable, and ready for one more step.

seed_pool.opening_token: Dare someone to carry a spoon across the room.
Dare someone to make a paper hat and wear it to the other side of the room.
Dare someone to stack three cushions and move them one at a time.

action: move it from one chair to another
place it on a marked spot
pass it from one hand to the other
bring it back without dropping it
setting: from the sofa to the door
from one marked spot to another

tests: One short sentence with one harmless object, one clear action, and one ordinary setting.
The dare is safe for a family room. No climbing, running, touching strangers, dangerous objects, humiliation, or damage.
A stranger can tell what the person must do within five seconds.
The starting dare is easy enough to accept and has room for several harder rules.
Everyday words a twelve-year-old knows. No brand names, street names, real people, or private information.

move_constraints.example: Do it while wearing oven mitts.
move_constraints.hint: Add exactly one harder rule to the same dare. Keep every rung already there and leave room for another.

rubric.name: squeeze
rubric.description: How much the new rule makes the same dare harder, while keeping it safe and possible.
rubric.anchors: 0 = no extra difficulty, it changes nothing; 1 = a tiny nuisance, such as using the other hand; 2 = a clear obstacle, such as moving slowly or keeping one hand behind the back; 3 = a strong but fair challenge that makes success uncertain; 4 = a precise, safe, and memorable obstacle that makes the next rung a tight fit, rare. A dangerous, impossible, or wildly unrelated rule scores 1 at most.

rubric.name: fits
rubric.description: Whether the rule keeps the same dare and preserves every earlier rule.
rubric.anchors: 0 = replaces the dare, removes a rule, or contradicts the ladder; 1 = vaguely related but skips the link or changes the task; 2 = keeps the task and adds a workable rule; 3 = clearly builds on every earlier rung and leaves a next step; 4 = adds a neat escalation that makes an earlier rule matter more, rare. A rule that finishes the dare completely scores 1 at most.

rubric.name: colour
rubric.description: How clearly and playfully the new rule lets someone picture the dare.
rubric.anchors: 0 = unclear or dull; 1 = one plain instruction; 2 = easy to picture; 3 = visual and funny without making the person the joke; 4 = instantly pictureable, safe, and delightfully awkward, rare. Fancy wording never wins here.

criterion.description: A move HOLDS if it adds exactly one doable escalation to the same dare, keeps every earlier rule, and leaves a clear next step. A move BREAKS the ladder if it skips several levels of difficulty without a bridge, replaces the original action with a new dare, removes or weakens a standing rule, makes the task unsafe or impossible, or completes the dare so there is no sensible next rung. The new rule must make the same task harder, not merely add decoration. A safe, precise obstacle scores well. A vague rule may hold but scores low. The points go to the move's useful pressure, faithful building, and clear picture.
criterion.anti_metagaming_clause: Talking to the host about the game, the rules, or how the partner is playing, instead of adding one dare rule, is itself a broken ladder.
judge_notes: On a FIRST move there are no earlier added rules: judge the move against the card alone. It must add one safe, doable escalation to the starting dare and leave room for another rung.
The full transcript is the ladder. Check the new rule against every earlier rule, not only the last one.
A skipped link fails when the move jumps from a gentle task to a much harder version with no single obstacle that explains the increase. When the increase is modest and clear, it holds.

An ending fails when the move declares the dare finished, says the task is complete, or otherwise leaves no clear next step. A move may make success very hard, but it must still be possible to add another rule.
An undo fails when the move removes, relaxes, cancels, or contradicts a standing rule, even if it adds a new obstacle elsewhere.
A new dare fails when it changes the main object or action instead of adding one rule to the existing task. A small change in how the same task is done may hold.

Safety is a gate. Reject rules involving dangerous heights, traffic, fire, sharp objects, harmful substances, forced contact, strangers, property damage, or serious embarrassment. When wording can be read safely, use the safe reading.
Exactly one new rule is required. Several linked restrictions in one move count as a skipped link unless they form one ordinary, inseparable instruction.
A detail that repeats an earlier rule without making the dare harder is a duplicate: not_semantic_duplicate is false.

voice_rules: One sentence, under 140 characters. Two short sentences at most.
The joke carries the reason. A stranger who read only the ladder and the new rule must see why it held or broke.
Name the new rule or its plain stand-in. A headline that fits any other dare is a bad headline.
Never open with a status word or a ruling phrase. No "Holds", "Broken", "Accepted", "Refused", "The Ladder Keeper rules".
No dashes as punctuation, no colons after a verdict, no ellipses. Commas and full stops only.
Jokes target the move, never the player. No comments about identity, body, family, intelligence, spelling, or worth.
Plain spoken English, a cheerful challenge, not a grand adventure story. No poetry, no rhymes, no fancy words.
On a break the headline puts the standing rule beside the new rule that removed it, skipped too far, changed the dare, or ended the ladder.
On a refusal, a gate failure, the headline refuses the move and asks for another. It never rules on who won.
The coaching line names one safe rule that would have held and made the same dare harder. It ends on a fact, never a mood.
good_headlines: Oven mitts on, spoon still crossing. That is one tidy rung, and the spoon is already nervous.
Elbows tucked after the mitts. The ladder climbs, though the arms have filed a complaint.
The book, hop, and backwards alphabet arrive together. That is three rungs in a trench coat.
Bare hands remove the mitt rule. The ladder cannot climb by taking its own steps away.
The garden replaces the room. Same spoon, different dare, and the ladder noticed.
You called it complete before the next rule. A ladder needs somewhere to put its foot.
One hand behind the back would have held and left the spoon crossing the room.
Slow steps would have raised the difficulty without asking the spoon to become a circus act.
The mitts stay, the elbows stay, and one new balance rule joins them. That is a proper rung.
No fireworks needed, just carry the spoon with your weaker hand. The room is still waiting.

bad_headlines.text: Holds: the new rule is fine.
bad_headlines.why: opens with a status word and gives no picture

bad_headlines.text: The Ladder Keeper rules that this rung breaks.
bad_headlines.why: opens with a ruling phrase and names the host
names no rule and gives no reason

bad_headlines.text: Only a silly person would suggest that.
bad_headlines.why: mocks the player instead of the move

bad_headlines.text: The ladder trembles beneath a thunderous mountain of challenge.
bad_headlines.why: uses grand, poetic language instead of plain speech

bad_headlines.text: Maybe it holds, maybe it does not, depending on how you look at it.
bad_headlines.why: hedges instead of giving a clear ruling

bad_headlines.text: Accepted, and the oven mitts are funny.
bad_headlines.why: starts with a status word and explains too little
does not name the broken rule or explain the failure

bad_headlines.text: The ladder has become an existential staircase.
bad_headlines.why: is vague, fancy, and not family plain
judges the player and offers no useful reason

rules: Every card starts with one harmless dare. Build on that same dare.
One move adds exactly one harder rule. Keep every earlier rule.
A skipped link, an undo, a new dare, an unsafe rule, or an ending breaks the ladder.
A move must leave the dare possible and leave room for another rung.
Points go to clear, safe escalations that make the existing task harder without changing it.

labels.compose_waiting: Draft your next rung while you wait

validation_messages.empty: Nothing added. The Ladder Keeper is waiting.
validation_messages.too_long: Over 140 characters. One rung, not a whole staircase.
validation_messages.duplicate: That rule is already on the ladder. Add a new obstacle.
validation_messages.nudge: Twice now. Add one safe rule that keeps {standing_form} and makes the same dare harder. Do not undo it or end the ladder.

judge_out_text: The Ladder Keeper has stepped out. Nobody adds a rung until they are back. {standing_form} is still the last step. Give it a moment.
opponent_prompt:
You are one of two friends building a ridiculous but safe dare, rung by rung.
One rule per turn, in one or two plain sentences.
Keep the original object and action. Never remove an earlier rule, replace the dare,
skip several levels, make the task unsafe, or declare it finished. Leave a clear next step.
The best move adds one obstacle that is easy to understand and still possible. Try a
slower pace, the other hand, a simple balance, a funny position, a quiet voice, or a
small restriction on movement. Keep all earlier rules exactly as they are.
Good: "Do it while wearing oven mitts." / "Keep both elbows tucked against your sides."
Bad: "Also hop, sing backwards, balance a book, and spin" because it skips several rungs.
Bad: "Take off the mitts" because it removes a rule. Bad: "Now do it in the garden"
because it changes the dare. Bad: "That rule is unfair" because it talks about the game
instead of adding a rule.
Use family safe ideas. No heights, traffic, fire, sharp objects, harmful substances,
forced touching, strangers, property damage, or serious embarrassment. Talk like a
person making a silly challenge in a living room, not like a novelist. Never repeat a
rule already used this match. Build directly on the standing form and leave the dare
ready for one more rung.
default_move: Do it with your weaker hand, while keeping every rule already on the ladder.
